desc:
An undirected graph has nodes 0 to n - 1 and the edge list edges (edge number i is edges[i] = [u, v]). Then edges are deleted one at a time: removals[k] is the index of the edge deleted in the k-th step. Every index appears at most once, and edges that are never listed stay forever.

Return an array whose k-th element is the number of connected components of the graph right after the k-th deletion.

n = 5
edges = [[0,1],[1,2],[2,3],[3,4],[0,2]]
removals = [4,1,2]

result = [1,2,3]

Deleting edge 4 (0-2) leaves the path 0-1-2-3-4 (one component). Deleting edge 1 (1-2) splits it into {0,1} and {2,3,4}. Deleting edge 2 (2-3) leaves {0,1}, {2}, {3,4}.
constraints: edges[i] = [u, v] with 0 ≤ u, v < n and u ≠ v; parallel edges are allowed
removals contains distinct valid edge indices
hints: Union-find supports merging sets, but it cannot undo a merge. Deleting edges looks like the wrong direction for it.
Run time backwards. Going backwards, deleting an edge becomes adding that edge.

Start from the graph that contains only the edges never deleted and count its components. Then walk through removals from the last to the first: record the current count as the answer of that step, and afterwards add that edge back (union; decrement the count if it merges two sets).
editorial: Deleting edges from a union-find structure is not supported, but adding them is. So reverse the process. Build a union-find from all edges that are never removed; its component count is the state after the very last deletion.

Now iterate over removals from the end towards the start. At position k the current structure is exactly the graph right after deletion k, so store the current component count as result[k]. Then put the edge removals[k] back by uniting its endpoints (subtracting one from the count if they were in different sets); this gives the graph right after deletion k - 1. Total time is O((n + m) · α(n)) with m edges. This offline 'reverse time' trick is the standard way to handle deletions with union-find.
